P1_June2019_Q1|-|text: f(x) = 3x^3 + 2*a*x^2 - 4x + 5a. Given that (x + 3) is a factor of f(x), find the value of the constant a.
P1_June2019_Q1|-|ms: M1: attempts f(-3) = 3(-3)^3 + 2a(-3)^2 - 4(-3) + 5a = 0 (or uses algebraic long division to find the remainder in terms of a, set to 0). M1: solves the resulting linear equation in a: 23a - 69 = 0 => a = ... A1: a = 3 (correct solution only). (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q2|stem: Figure 1 shows a plot of part of the curve with equation y = cos(x), where x is measured in radians. Diagram 1 is a copy of Figure 1.
P1_June2019_Q2|a|text: (a) Use Diagram 1 to show why the equation cos(x) - 2x - 1/2 = 0 has only one real root, giving a reason for your answer. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q2|a|ms: (a) B1: draws the line y = 2x + 1/2 on the diagram, with an attempt at the correct gradient and correct intercept. B1: explains that, because there is only one intersection between this line and y=cos(x) on the diagram, there is just one root (requires a reason and a minimal conclusion). (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q2|b|text: Given that the root of the equation is alpha, and that alpha is small, (b) use the small angle approximation for cos(x) to estimate the value of alpha to 3 decimal places. (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q2|b|ms: (b) M1: attempts to use the small angle approximation cos(x) ≈ 1 - x^2/2 in the given equation, reaching a single-variable 3-term-quadratic equation. dM1: proceeds to solve the resulting 3TQ: 1 - x^2/2 - 2x - 1/2 = 0, rearranging to x^2 + 4x - 1 = 0. A1: alpha = -2 + sqrt(5) ≈ 0.236 (to 3 decimal places). (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q3|a|text: (a) Show that dy/dx = A/(x+1)^n, where A and n are constants to be found. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q3|a|ms: (a) M1: attempts a correct method to differentiate (quotient rule and chain rule, or product rule and chain rule, or rewrites as y=5-5(x+1)^-2 and uses the chain rule directly). A1: a correct (possibly unsimplified) derivative. M1: valid attempt to simplify/factorise and cancel a common (x+1) factor. A1: dy/dx = 10/(x+1)^3, [editor: i.e. A=10, n=3]. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q3|b|text: (b) Hence deduce the range of values for x for which dy/dx < 0. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q3|b|ms: (b) B1ft: deduces x < -1 (follow through on their A/(x+1)^n with A>0 [editor: — dy/dx<0 requires (x+1)^n<0, i.e. x+1<0 for odd n=3]). (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q4|a|text: (a) Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of x, of the binomial expansion of 1/sqrt(4-x), giving each coefficient in its simplest form. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q4|a|ms: (a) M1: for the strategy of expanding 1/sqrt(4-x) as 4^(-1/2)*(1-x/4)^(-1/2), i.e. must see 4^(-1/2) taken out. M1: uses a correct binomial expansion for (1-x/4)^(-1/2) = 1 + (-1/2)(-x/4) + [(-1/2)(-3/2)/2](-x/4)^2 + ... A1: correct unsimplified expansion. A1: simplified to 1/2 + x/16 + 3x^2/256. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q4|b(i)|text: The expansion can be used to find an approximation to sqrt(2). Possible values of x that could be substituted into this expansion are: x = -14 because 1/sqrt(4-x) = 1/sqrt(18) = sqrt(2)/6; x = 2 because 1/sqrt(4-x) = 1/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2)/2; x = -1/2 because 1/sqrt(4-x) = 1/sqrt(9/2) = sqrt(2)/3. (b) Without evaluating your expansion, (i) state, giving a reason, which of the three values of x should not be used (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q4|b(i)|ms: (b)(i) B1: states x = -14 should not be used, with a valid reason, e.g. the expansion is only valid for |x| < 4, and 14 > 4. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q4|b(ii)|text: (ii) state, giving a reason, which of the three values of x would lead to the most accurate approximation to sqrt(2) (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q4|b(ii)|ms: (b)(ii) B1: states x = -1/2 would give the most accurate approximation, with a valid reason, e.g. it is the value closest to zero [editor: (of the two remaining valid choices)], which gives the most accurate truncated approximation. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q5|a|text: (a) Write f(x) in the form a(x+b)^2 + c, where a, b and c are integers to be found. (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q5|a|ms: (a) B1: achieves 2x^2+4x+9 = 2(x+k)^2 + ... or states a=2. M1: deals correctly with the first two terms, reaching 2(x+1)^2 + ... (i.e. b=1). A1: 2x^2+4x+9 = 2(x+1)^2 + 7 (so a=2, b=1, c=7). (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q5|b|text: (b) Sketch the curve with equation y = f(x), showing any points of intersection with the coordinate axes and the coordinates of any turning point. (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q5|b|ms: (b) B1: sketches a U-shaped curve in any position, not passing through the origin. B1: correct y-intercept marked at (0,9). B1ft: correct minimum marked at (-1,7), in the correct quadrant (follow through on their a(x+b)^2+c). (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q5|c|text: (c)(i) Describe fully the transformation that maps the curve with equation y = f(x) onto the curve with equation y = g(x), where g(x) = 2(x-2)^2 + 4x - 3. (ii) Find the range of the function h(x) = 21/(2x^2+4x+9). (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q5|c|ms: (c)(i) M1: deduces a translation with one correct aspect (simplifying g(x) to vertex form 2(x-1)^2+3 and comparing to f(x)'s vertex form, or an equivalent method). A1: fully describes the transformation as a translation by vector (2, -4) (2 units right, 4 units down) — both 'translate' and the correct vector must be given. (c)(ii) M1: correct attempt at finding the maximum value of h(x), using the minimum value of f(x) found in part (a): h(x) = 21/f(x), [editor: maximum of h occurs at the minimum of f,] giving 21/7 = 3. A1ft: states the range as 0 < h(x) <= 3 (follow through on their value of c from part (a), giving max value 21/c). (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q6|a|text: (a) Solve, for -180 degrees <= theta <= 180 degrees, the equation 5*sin(2*theta) = 9*tan(theta), giving your answers, where necessary, to one decimal place. (Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.) (6 marks)
P1_June2019_Q6|a|ms: (a) M1: attempts the overall strategy of forming an equation in one trigonometric function, using sin(2theta) = 2*sin(theta)*cos(theta) and tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta). A1: uses these identities correctly to form a correct simplified equation, e.g. 10*sin(theta)*cos^2(theta) = 9*sin(theta), leading to sin(theta)*(10*cos^2(theta) - 9) = 0, or an equivalent form such as 10*cos^2(theta) = 9 [editor: (after dividing by sin(theta), noting sin(theta)=0 gives theta=0,180 separately)]. dM1: uses the correct order of operations to find at least one value of theta from cos(theta) = ±sqrt(9/10). A1: any one of the four non-trivial values, awrt ±18.4 or ±161.6. A1: all four values awrt ±18.4, ±161.6 found (and no extras beyond these plus 0 and 180). B1: theta = 0, 180 also included as solutions [editor: (from the sin(theta)=0 branch)] — can be scored independently. (6 marks)
P1_June2019_Q6|b|text: (b) Deduce the smallest positive solution to the equation 5*sin(2x - 50 degrees) = 9*tan(x - 25 degrees). (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q6|b|ms: (b) M1: attempts to solve x - 25 = theta_solution, using one of their values of theta from part (a) [editor: (specifically theta = -18.4, since the equation is theta = x-25 shifted)]. A1ft: x = awrt 6.6 (the smallest positive solution). (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q7|stem: In a simple model, the value, £V, of a car depends on its age, t, in years. The following information is available for car A: its value when new is £20,000; its value after one year is £16,000.
P1_June2019_Q7|a|text: (a) Use an exponential model to form, for car A, a possible equation linking V with t. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q7|a|ms: (a) M1: uses a model of the form V = A*e^(-kt) (k not fixed to a specific value). M1: substitutes t=0, V=20000 to find A=20000. dM1: substitutes t=1, V=16000 into 16000=20000*e^(-k) and uses logs to find k. A1: V = 20000*e^(-0.223t) (accuracy to at least 3sf), or equivalently V=20000*(0.8)^t. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q7|b|text: The value of car A is monitored over a 10-year period. Its value after 10 years is £2,000. (b) Evaluate the reliability of your model in light of this information. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q7|b|ms: (b) M1: uses the model to find V at t=10: V = 20000*e^(-2.23) ≈ £2150. A1: compares £2150 with the actual £2000 and makes a suitable reliability comment, e.g. 'reasonably reliable since £2150 is close to £2000' (a candidate arguing unreliable with a suitable reason can also be credited). (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q7|c|text: The following information is available for car B: it has the same value, when new, as car A; its value depreciates more slowly than that of car A. (c) Explain how you would adapt the equation found in (a) so that it could be used to model the value of car B. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q7|c|ms: (c) B1ft: states that the value of the decay constant (their '0.223', or equivalently the base if using a power model) should be made less negative / closer to 1, [editor: so that the value depreciates more slowly]. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q8|stem: Figure 2 shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation y = x(x+2)(x-4). The region R1 shown shaded is bounded by the curve and the negative x-axis.
P1_June2019_Q8|a|text: (a) Show that the exact area of R1 is 20/3. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q8|a|ms: (a) B1: expands x(x+2)(x-4) to x^3 - 2x^2 - 8x. M1: correct attempt at integrating the cubic (power increased by 1 on at least two terms). dM1: correct strategy for the area of R1 — integrates between -2 and 0 [editor: and takes the modulus (since the curve is above the x-axis on this interval, the definite integral itself is already positive here)]. A1*: rigorous argument showing the integral evaluates to 20/3, with the limits the correct way round and values shown. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q8|b|text: The region R2, also shown shaded, is bounded by the curve, the positive x-axis, and the line with equation x=b, where b is a positive constant and 0 < b < 4. Given that the area of R1 is equal to the area of R2, (b) verify that b satisfies the equation (b+2)^2 * (3*b^2 - 20*b + 20) = 0 (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q8|b|ms: (b) M1: sets their integrated expression evaluated between 0 and b equal to -20/3 [editor: (since R2 lies below the axis for 0<x<4, so the definite integral itself is negative there, equal in magnitude to the area 20/3)]. A1: correctly deduces 3b^4 - 8b^3 - 48b^2 + 80 = 0 (integer coefficients). M1: attempts to factorise this quartic, extracting a factor of (b+2)^2 by inspection or repeated division. A1*: correctly reaches (b+2)^2 * (3b^2-20b+20) = 0 with no errors. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q8|c|text: The roots of the equation 3*b^2 - 20*b + 20 = 0 are 1.225 and 5.442 to 3 decimal places. The value of b is therefore 1.225 to 3 decimal places. (c) Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the significance of the root 5.442 (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q8|c|ms: (c) B1: sketches the curve with a vertical line drawn to the right of x=4 (at x=5.442, which may not be explicitly labelled). B1: gives a valid explanation of the root's significance, explaining that between x = -2 and x = 5.442 the area above the x-axis equals the area below the x-axis, or equivalent (candidates may express this in various equivalent correct forms, e.g. 'the area between x=1.225 and x=4 equals the area between x=4 and x=5.442', or 'the net signed area from x=0 to x=5.442 is 20/3') with the areas appropriately shaded/labelled on the diagram. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q9|stem: Given that a > b > 0 and that a and b satisfy the equation log(a) - log(b) = log(a-b),
P1_June2019_Q9|a|ms: (a) B1: states or uses log(a) - log(b) = log(a/b), giving a/b = a - b. M1: attempts to make 'a' the subject, collecting both terms in a on one side: a/b = a - b => ... => ab - a = b^2, then a(b-1) = b^2. A1*: correct solution only (cso), showing clear reasoning with no errors to a = b^2/(b-1). (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q9|b|text: (b) Write down the full restriction on the value of b, explaining the reason for this restriction. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q9|b|ms: (b) B1: deduces b > 1 (or states b ≠ 1 with a reason, e.g. 'a is undefined/infinite when b=1 since you cannot divide by 0'). B1: states the full restriction b > 1, explaining that since a > 0 and b^2 > 0, we need (b-1) > 0. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q10|i|text: (i) Prove that for all n (a positive integer), n^2 + 2 is not divisible by 4. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q10|i|ms: (i) M1: sets up the proof for one case (either n even or n odd), e.g. for n=2m: n^2+2 = 4m^2+2. A1: correctly concludes this case cannot be divisible by 4 [editor: (for n even, 4m^2+2 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 4)]. dM1: sets up the proof for the other case, e.g. for n=2m+1: n^2+2 = 4m^2+4m+3 = 4(m^2+m)+3. A1*: fully correct proof for both cases with valid explanation (remainder 3 mod 4 for odd n) and an overall concluding statement 'hence true for all n'. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q10|ii|text: (ii) Given x is real, the value of |3x - 28| is greater than or equal to the value of (x - 9). State, giving a reason, if the above statement is always true, sometimes true, or never true. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q10|ii|ms: (ii) M1: states or implies 'sometimes true' (or 'not always true') and gives a specific numerical example where the statement is FALSE, e.g. x=9.4: |3(9.4)-28| = 0.2, which is less than (9.4-9)=0.4, so false here. A1: gives a further example where the statement IS true, e.g. x=12: |36-28|=8, which is greater than (12-9)=3, so true here — concluding 'sometimes true'. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q11|stem: A competitor is running a 20 kilometre race. She runs each of the first 4 kilometres at a steady pace of 6 minutes per kilometre. After the first 4 kilometres, she begins to slow down: the time she takes to complete each subsequent kilometre is modelled to be 5% greater than the time she took to complete the previous kilometre. Using the model,
P1_June2019_Q11|a|text: (a) show that her time to run the first 6 kilometres is estimated to be 36 minutes 55 seconds (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q11|a|ms: (a) M1: uses the model to calculate the total time for 6km: 24 minutes (first 4km) + 6*1.05 + 6*1.05^2 minutes. A1*: correctly evaluates to 36.915 minutes = 36 minutes 55 seconds (given answer, so working must be fully shown). (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q11|b|text: (b) show that her estimated time, in minutes, to run the r-th kilometre, for 5 <= r <= 20, is 6*(1.05)^(r-4) (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q11|b|ms: (b) B1: makes the link between the r-th km (for r from 5 to 20) and the index of 1.05, i.e. explains that the 5th km is 6*1.05^1, the 6th is 6*1.05^2, etc., so the r-th km (r>=5) is 6*1.05^(r-4). (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q11|c|text: (c) estimate the total time, in minutes and seconds, that she will take to complete the race. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q11|c|ms: (c) M1: overall strategy — total time = 24 (minutes, for first 4km) + sum of the geometric series for km 5 to 20. M1: attempts to use the geometric series sum formula a(r^n-1)/(r-1) with the correct common ratio r=1.05, to find an allowable sum, e.g. first term a=6.3, n=16 terms, giving sum ≈ 149.04 minutes. A1: correct calculation shown that leads to the total time: 24 + 149.04. A1: total time = awrt 173 minutes and 3 seconds. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q12|a|text: (a) Show that the x coordinates of the turning points of the curve with equation y = f(x) satisfy the equation tan(x) = 4 (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q12|a|ms: (a) M1: attempts to differentiate using the product rule (and chain rule for the exponential term): f'(x) = -2.5*e^(-x/4)*sin(x) + 10*e^(-x/4)*cos(x) (condoning slips). A1: correct (possibly unsimplified) f'(x). M1: sets f'(x)=0, factors out and cancels the common e^(-x/4) term, leading to an equation purely in sin(x) and cos(x). A1*: shows the steps -2.5*sin(x)+10*cos(x)=0 => sin(x)/cos(x) = 10/2.5, leading to tan(x)=4, with all steps shown. (4 marks)
P1_June2019_Q12|b|text: Figure 3 shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation y = f(x). (b) Sketch the graph of H against t where H(t) = |10*e^(-t/4)*sin(t)|, t >= 0, showing the long-term behaviour of this curve. (2 marks) The function H(t) is used to model the height, in metres, of a ball above the ground t seconds after it has been kicked.
P1_June2019_Q12|b|ms: (b) M1: sketches at least two 'loops' (bounces), with the height of the second loop lower than the first. A1: at least 4 loops shown with decreasing heights, no rounding at the cusps [editor: (curve meets the t-axis at t=0,pi,2pi,3pi,... with sharp points, envelope decaying)]. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q12|c|text: Using this model, find (c) the maximum height of the ball above the ground between the first and second bounce. (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q12|c|ms: (c) M1: understands that they need to solve tan(t)=4 [editor: for the turning point between the 1st bounce (t=pi) and 2nd bounce (t=2pi), i.e. t = pi + arctan(4) ≈ 4.47]. M1: substitutes t ≈ 4.47 into H(t) = 10*e^(-t/4)*|sin(t)|. A1: awrt 3.18 (metres). (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q12|d|text: (d) Explain why this model should not be used to predict the time of each bounce. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q12|d|ms: (d) B1: makes reference to the fact that the time between each bounce should NOT stay the same (constant, at pi seconds apart) when the height of each bounce is getting smaller — in reality bounces would become more frequent as the height decreases[editor: , which this model does not capture]. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q13|stem: The curve C with equation y = (p - 3x) / [(2x - q)(x + 3)], x is real, x != -3, x != 2, where p and q are constants, passes through the point (3, 1/2) and has two vertical asymptotes with equations x=2 and x=-3.
P1_June2019_Q13|a|text: (a)(i) Explain why you can deduce that q = 4 (ii) Show that p = 15 (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q13|a|ms: (a)(i) B1*: explains that the asymptote at x=2 occurs where the factor (2x-q)=0, so 2(2)-q=0, giving q=4. (a)(ii) M1: substitutes the point (3, 1/2) into y=(p-3x)/[(2x-4)(x+3)] and solves for p. A1*: full proof showing (p-9)/[(2)(6)]=1/2 => p-9=6 => p=15, with all steps shown. (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q13|b|text: Figure 4 shows a sketch of part of the curve C. The region R, shown shaded, is bounded by the curve C, the x-axis, and the line with equation x=3. (b) Show that the exact value of the area of R is a*ln(2) + b*ln(3), where a and b are rational constants to be found. (8 marks)
P1_June2019_Q13|b|ms: (b) M1: overall attempt at using partial fractions and integrating with logs, with sight of the limits 3 and another value. M1: writes (15-3x)/[(2x-4)(x+3)] = A/(2x-4) + B/(x+3) and solves for A and B. A1: A=1.8, B=-2.4 (or equivalent unsimplified form). M1: integrates to the form m*ln(2x-4) + n*ln(x+3). A1ft: correct integral 0.9*ln(2x-4) - 2.4*ln(x+3), follow through on their A and B. B1: deduces the limits for the integral are 3 and 5 [editor: (the curve crosses the x-axis, i.e. numerator=0, at x=5, giving the upper limit; the region starts at the given line x=3)]. dM1: uses correct log work to express the result in terms of ln(2) and ln(3) (e.g. ln(6)=ln(2)+ln(3), ln(8)=3*ln(2)). A1: Area = 3.3*ln(3) - 4.8*ln(2) (i.e. a=-4.8, b=3.3). (8 marks)
P1_June2019_Q14|stem: The curve C, in the standard Cartesian plane, is defined by the equation x = 4*sin(2y), -pi/4 < y < pi/4. The curve C passes through the origin O.
P1_June2019_Q14|a|text: (a) Find the value of dy/dx at the origin. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q14|a|ms: (a) M1: attempts to differentiate x=4sin(2y) with respect to y and inverts: dx/dy = 8cos(2y), so dy/dx = 1/(8cos(2y)). A1: at the origin (y=0), dy/dx = 1/8. (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q14|b|text: (b)(i) Use the small angle approximation for sin(2y) to find an equation linking x and y for points close to the origin. (ii) Explain the relationship between the answers to (a) and (b)(i). (2 marks)
P1_June2019_Q14|b|ms: (b)(i) B1: uses sin(2y) ≈ 2y for small y, to obtain x ≈ 8y. (1 mark) (b)(ii) B1: explains that the value found in part (a), 1/8, is the gradient of the linear approximation line found in (b)(i) [editor: (x=8y, i.e. y=x/8, which has gradient 1/8) — the small-angle approximation's tangent line has the same gradient as the curve at the origin]. (1 mark)
P1_June2019_Q14|c|text: (c) Show that, for all points (x,y) lying on C, dy/dx = 1/(a*sqrt(b - x^2)), where a and b are constants to be found. (3 marks)
P1_June2019_Q14|c|ms: (c) M1: uses their dy/dx as a function of y, together with sin^2(2y)+cos^2(2y)=1 and x=4sin(2y), to write dy/dx (or dx/dy) as a function of x. A1: a correct unsimplified answer, e.g. dy/dx = 1/[8*sqrt(1-(x/4)^2)]. A1: dy/dx = 1/[2*sqrt(16-x^2)] (i.e. a=2, b=16), in the correct simplified form. (3 marks)
